paras: The Lawrenceville grave-dancing deaths were the deaths of three young men at Lawrenceville, Illinois, reported in February 1882, who fled from mourners preparing to lynch them after they had danced at a friend's grave. Escaping down the river in a leaky boat, they were left stranded on the bank when it sank, and they were found dead of cold and exhaustion. The story circulated as a short unsigned paragraph in miscellany columns from February to May 1882.

According to the paragraph, three "young fellows" decided to dance at the grave of a friend at Lawrenceville, and one of them fell into it. Their conduct "shocked the mourners," who drove them away and "subsequently prepared to lynch them"; a reworded version said the "friends in attendance" drove them from the cemetery and that "arrangements were subsequently made to lynch them." No attack on the men is described, and the number of mourners is not given.

The three fled in a leaky boat and went down the river, fourteen miles in the earlier text and "several miles" in the rewording, before the boat sank under them. They swam to shore on a cold night but were too exhausted to go farther, and their bodies were found in the morning, near the spot where they had landed.
None of the printings names the men or the mourners, gives the race of either, or mentions an inquest, arrests or any official action.

The earliest printing found appeared in the Daily Gazette on 14 February 1882, and the same wording ran the next day in the Evening Critic, which placed the town in "Ind." The paragraph reached the Gold Hill Daily News in Nevada on 21 February, and on 1 March the Eureka Daily Sentinel printed it under the headline "A Melancholy Story." The People and New Hampshire Patriot of Concord included it on 23 March among "Some Curious Things That Have Come to Pass," and the Seattle Daily Post-Intelligencer reprinted it as late as 5 May; both omitted the distance.

The Juniata Sentinel and Republican rewrote the item among its "General Items," calling the men "Three foolish young fellows." None of the papers commented on the planned lynching, and the item ran among miscellany as a curiosity rather than as news of mob violence.

No one was killed by the mourners: the papers say the three young men died of cold and exhaustion after their boat sank while they fled a planned lynching (A1, A6). The mourners' number is not given, and the only motive stated is that the men's conduct 'shocked' them (A1).
Every printing found is one unsourced paragraph (A1) or a light rewording of it (A6), with no local report, names or follow-up.
